item.title: Pentagon looks to build a deep-cover spy program to confront China
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Pentagon has spent months quietly building an elite new tech agency to help covertly disrupt and sabotage foreign technology programs considered threats to American military superiority. Neither Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth nor any other senior Pentagon official has publicly mentioned the agency since it was established this April — a conspicuous omission for a department that has reveled in announcing other major changes aimed at modernizing the military or adopting hard-nosed new policies against foreign adversaries. Information on the Technology Support Office, or TSO as it is called internally, is nearly impossible to find on Pentagon websites, and the agency is mentioned by name only in several previously unreported Defense Department historical records and memoranda . While the specifics of its work are highly classified, POLITICO spoke with 12 current and former U.S. national security officials with varying degrees of knowledge about TSO to understand how the agency came to be, the broad contours of its mission and why its operations are shrouded in secrecy. Some of these people helped establish TSO or worked closely with it; others attended briefings or spoke with current Pentagon officials about it; and some were familiar with Defense Department intelligence programs now merged into TSO. All were granted anonymity to share sensitive details about the agency that have not been previously reported. Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, a private equity billionaire and former head of the White House's Intelligence Advisory Board during President Donald Trump's first term, led the push inside the Pentagon to create the new agency. Tom Rakusan, a senior adviser to Feinberg at the Pentagon, has also been closely involved in setting up TSO. Rakusan is a longtime veteran of the CIA's clandestine service, and most recently worked at Feinberg's private equity firm, where he focused on emerging technology. Hegseth and Feinberg established TSO quickly and without attracting outside scrutiny because they largely built the agency by reorganizing two classified Pentagon intelligence programs that have conducted similar clandestine tech-sabotage efforts at a smaller scale since 2023. But by creating an agency dedicated to expanding that work, the Defense Department is signaling its intent to ramp up a range of aggressive covert activities abroad — potentially including cyberattacks, supply chain disruptions and disinformation operations. Many of the people who spoke to POLITICO argued that the aggressive new initiative is needed to help the Pentagon counter foreign adversaries they say are harnessing artificial intelligence and advanced commercial technologies, such as drones, in creative ways that could erode America's military advantage. "It is a refocus from the highest levels of the government on this type of activity, which has been sorely needed," said one former senior Pentagon intelligence official with direct knowledge of TSO. Others worry that the Trump administration has deliberately avoided public mention of TSO to avoid oversight over programs that could harm civilians or inflame tensions with adversary countries the U.S. is not at war with, such as China. To make an undertaking like TSO successful, said another former senior Pentagon official, "you have to pull off movie-level spy craft." "But the questions are: What are the approval structures, what is the oversight, who is read in to give the American people confidence that what you're doing is consistent with our values and you're not creating something that five years from now will be seen as incredibly problematic?" the official added. In response to a series of questions about TSO and the details of this story, Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss said, "This query appears to be built on information that is simply not true. Whoever is feeding you these claims are either badly misinformed or deliberately leading you astray to peddle their fantasies." The White House did not respond to a request for comment on this story. A move to 'centralize' control While TSO lacks the legal authority to conduct clandestine operations directly, it works closely with senior U.S. military and intelligence officers to develop cutting-edge tools and strategies to disrupt adversaries' access to critical defense technologies — or subvert them from afar. TSO is staffed with engineers, special operators and intelligence officers, and its work spans everything from building bespoke hacking tools to planning elaborate deception operations that trick adversaries into installing faulty components — likely designed by TSO — in key foreign weapons platforms. TSO's overarching goal is to "buy time or stop adversaries from developing technologies" that would most threaten the U.S. military in a major conflict, said a former U.S. intelligence official who worked closely with the agency. Pentagon staff had been exploring whether to create a new agency like TSO for more than a year. According to three former intelligence officials, staff in the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, or I&S, which oversees Defense Department intelligence programs, began work in early 2025 on a white paper exploring how to scale up the Pentagon's two existing classified tech sabotage programs. The white paper, completed that fall, considered nesting both programs under the Pentagon's digital warfighting unit, U.S. Cyber Command, but ultimately recommended merging the efforts into a new agency with its own budget and procurement powers. The move would empower the agency to more quickly integrate cutting-edge tech from the private sector and think more strategically about which foreign defense technologies pose the biggest threats across U.S. military organizations. Senior Pentagon leadership also saw an opportunity to consolidate some control over Defense Department intelligence programs, a former Pentagon official familiar with the initiative said. TSO is "definitely part of this move to centralize some control upstairs," the official explained. A new Pentagon power center The race to stand up the agency kicked off in earnest this spring. Feinberg signed a memo establishing TSO and placing it under the "authority, direction, and control" of the Undersecretary of War for Intelligence & Security on April 14, according to a monthly leadership publication from the Defense Department's public record-keeping office. The Senate confirmed the current head of I&S, Bradley Hansell, in July 2025. This summer, the Pentagon tapped Grant Hundley, a former Marine Corps special operations officer, to serve as TSO's director. They also selected William Nelson, a career Army official recently at Army Futures Command, as the new Director of Intelligence for Sensitive Activities and Special Programs, who will work with Hansell to oversee the agency internally from I&S. It's unclear how much money has been allocated to carry out TSO's secretive operations, or if it has issued any new contracts yet. A second former Pentagon official and a former U.S. national security official said the agency has told some defense contractors it's interested in offensive hacking capabilities. The former senior Pentagon intelligence official estimated that its budget for classified contracts alone is likely north of $1.5 billion. They are seeking contractors on "the leading edge of technology," that official said, and hope to procure "a whole host of tools wherever your imagination can go." Bliss did not respond to a request for comment on whether the Pentagon has requested additional money to fund the agency or if it intends to seek long-term authorization from Congress. Beyond offensive operations, TSO will also focus on coordinating technology use and cutting red tape for defense contractors spread across a thicket of heavily siloed Pentagon intelligence programs. According to one former U.S. intelligence official who has spoken with Pentagon leadership, one such initiative would see TSO build a central "catalog" of approved commercial AI and tech tools contractors could use on classified initiatives. The agency's emergence as a power center for military hacking and sabotage has irked some senior officials elsewhere in the Pentagon. Special Operations Command and U.S. Cyber Command both objected to creating the new agency, fearing it would cut into their budgets, according to the two former intelligence officials and one former senior U.S. national security official. The two former intelligence officials added that friction over TSO is part of the reason why Cyber Command's chief acquisition officer, Khoi Nguyen, recently left the command . Nguyen, whose former role had him overseeing the digital warfighting unit's efforts to procure cutting-edge hacking tools, did not reply to a request for comment. TSO, said the former intelligence official who worked closely with the agency, is taking on the types of operations Cyber Command "would love to claim as its own." 'Opportunities to hide and misdirect' Several people who spoke to POLITICO support TSO's mission but worry that the secrecy surrounding its work could embolden current Pentagon leadership to carry out missions that flout international law or funnel coveted classified contracts to political allies. Over the last two years, Hegseth has boasted publicly about operations that test the boundaries of domestic and international law , while slow-rolling Congressional attempts to oversee deadly missions that have gone awry. The Pentagon recently briefed some congressional officials on its plans for TSO, but only a small number of staffers have been read in on the initiative, said one current U.S. national security official, which could make it harder for Congress to identify any potential impropriety in TSO's operations or contracting. "Because it's a classified space, there's even more opportunities to hide or misdirect," the official said. In a statement, Bliss, the Pentagon spokesperson, said the Defense Department "values its longstanding working relationship with Congress" and "will continue working closely and constructively with the relevant committees to provide appropriate information, answer legitimate questions, and ensure Congress can fulfill its constitutional oversight responsibilities." Hegseth and Feinberg have announced a flurry of new modernization initiatives — such as a new commission dubbed Project Meridian led by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Anduril founder Palmer Luckey — that skeptics say expose the Defense Department to a torrent of conflicts of interest. Democrats have focused their concern on Feinberg because the private equity and venture capital firms he led before joining the Defense Department both have sizable investments in defense tech companies that compete for Pentagon contracts. Bliss called concern about conflicts of interest "a baseless, completely recycled narrative that certain reporters continue to lazily push despite having zero facts to support it." DOD, he added, "maintains a rigorous, multi-layered ethics framework that includes financial disclosure reviews, divestitures where appropriate, and screening to prevent conflicts of interest. Every DOW official is in full compliance with all ethical laws and regulations. Any claims otherwise are false." Other people who spoke to POLITICO said they felt reassured by the current and former career officials chosen to work most closely with the agency, specifically Nelson and Rakusan. These are "seasoned career professionals who have withstood political pressures before," said the former intelligence official who has spoken with Pentagon leadership about the initiative. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/pentagon-quietly-building-elite-tech-090000154.html

item.title: U.S. reportedly considering major strikes on Iran after the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The national flag of Iran hangs on a building damaged by the U.S.-Israeli attacks in Tehran, Iran, on April 20, 2026. —Shadati—Xinhua/Getty Images The U.S. and Israel are reportedly developing plans for major strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November. Citing people familiar with the deliberations, the New York Times reported on Wednesday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed the possibility of renewed strikes on Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel this week. Possible targets of the strikes reportedly include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment. U.S. officials have repeatedly asserted that the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps are teetering on the edge of collapse but are deliberately prolonging the war in an effort to meddle with Republican prospects in the midterm elections. Once the elections are over, President Donald Trump promised last month, the Iranian regime would quickly capitulate. “I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” Trump said. “They can’t hold out any longer.” Renewed strikes could complicate that outlook. Some officials have reportedly argued that resuming attacks for an intense but limited campaign would hasten Iran’s economic collapse, especially as the country has been squeezed by an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian ports and economic sanctions campaign . The officials hope the blow will make Iran more amenable to negotiations. Trump has at times shared that view. Last week, Trump told Newsmax he was considering additional military action in Iran, including a possible strike on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain , a nuclear facility deep underground. His comments came amid reports that he was weighing deploying a 22,000 GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, also known as the “mother of all bombs.” The President added the war would end soon, be it through negotiation or escalation. “Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month. “But I believe we’ll make a deal,” he added, “right after the election.” Will the U.S. renew strikes on Iran? Intensified fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels and the Saudi and Yemeni governments has threatened to create a broader regional crisis that could be harder to disengage from. The State Department on Wednesday ordered nonemergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia amid escalating attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure. Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and Aramco facilities, as well as their attempts to disrupt shipping through Bab El-Mandeb , which has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz for energy trade , could prompt direct U.S. strikes in support of Saudi Arabia, analysts have said. Trump said earlier this month that the U.S. “may” join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, although that has yet to transpire. Israel’s Oct. 27 election could also raise the stakes of additional military action. Netanyahu , whom Trump has endorsed , would remain in office until a new government is formed, even if his bloc loses the election, and his government would retain the authority to order strikes during that transition. But renewed strikes before the election, or after an electoral defeat, could invite scrutiny. “One ordered in the last weeks of a deadlocked campaign would be judged in Israel as politics as well as strategy,” Gregg Roman, executive director of the Middle East Forum, wrote in a September analysis. Nevertheless, the forum assessed that a large-scale Israeli strike on Iranian territory, with or without U.S. participation, was probable before the end of the year. Analysts told the Times Netanyahu could use the prospect of joint strikes to form a unity government that could allow him to stay in power. “The larger constraint,” Roman argued, “is Washington.” Trump has not yet approved the proposed strikes, the Times reported. Trump has also called off plans to renew attacks on Iran before. He reportedly blocked an Israeli plan for a multi-day offensive against Iran earlier this month, and rejected five proposals for major operations against Iran or the Houthis in recent months. The U.S. and Iran have not exchanged major fighting in recent weeks. The last reported U.S. strikes on Iran were on Sept. 8, even as Iranian attacks on commercial shipping have continued. Earlier this month, Trump ruled out attacking Iran before the midterms. Read More: What Is the Status of the U.S.-Iran Peace Talks? Here's What Both Sides Are Saying How might Iran respond to new strikes? Tehran’s reluctance to make concessions to the U.S. appears to have strengthened, rather than weakened, over the course of the war. Iranian leaders reiterated this week that they will not directly negotiate with the U.S. unless Washington accedes to certain demands , which include ending its naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds. The initial U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign on Iran that began the war on Feb. 28, as well as June 2025 attacks during an earlier round of U.S.-Iran nuclear diplomacy, also hardened the Iranian view that the U.S. is not serious about negotiating. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in March that the previous disruptions of negotiating rounds had increased distrust in Washington . Last month, the IRGC published an open letter appealing to American voters to “wrest control” from their government. In the letter, the IRGC said: “Despite all the hardships that our enemies impose on us, we will continue fighting, as we have done for the past 47 years.” Both the U.S. and Iran appear to believe they hold enough leverage to achieve their goals, and those “dueling perceptions” have impeded progress towards a deal, according to an Oct. 1 analysis by the New York-based nonpartisan research organization The Soufan Center. Iran’s key point of leverage is its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz , a narrow waterway vital to global energy trade. Iran’s militarization of the strait has disrupted global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, leading to soaring energy prices and inflation. Analysts previously told TIME that the higher prices are politically costly for Trump. In recent weeks, a growing number of Republicans have broken with Trump on Iran. The President has also seen his lowest approval ratings of his second term. Iran’s ability to choke off regional oil exports, however, appears to be waning. Middle East oil exports topped prewar levels last week as shipping companies use alternative routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. HSBC Group Chief Executive Georges Elhedery also projected that Hormuz could be “redundant” in five years thanks to investment in alternative logistics routes. Iranian officials told the Times that they are aware of the U.S. and Israel’s war planning and are developing their own tactics. Earlier this week, IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi told the Tehran Times that “even a limited” attack from Washington would provoke a “serious energy crisis” for the world. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said that an attack on Pickaxe Mountain would be met with a response “just as hard,” if not “stronger.” And earlier this month, Iranian officials said Iran had prepared potential retaliatory operations that would depart from the U.S. and Israel’s assumptions. Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei told Press TV that Iran could respond to renewed attacks by targeting new targets, including U.S.-linked data centers and AI facilities in the Gulf, as well as subsea communications cables. Last month, Iran threatened to retaliate against any further U.S. attacks by targeting U.S. oil and gas assets in the Gulf. Read More: ‘One of the World’s Most Critical Digital Bottlenecks’: How the Iran War Could Threaten Global Internet Access In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Mahdi Mohammadi, a senior adviser to Iran’s negotiator Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said, if the U.S. and Israel attack, “they may want to keep it short, but we will not allow it.” He added on Wednesday: “The war will continue longer and across a wider geography than the enemy calculates.” This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/10/22/us-israel-iran-war-strikes-midterms/

item.title: Websites worldwide go dark after AI discovers major security flaws
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model (ANDREJ IVANOV) Governments and companies around the world shut down websites as they raced Thursday to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP. PHP helps run about 70 percent of the world's websites -- from online stores and news outlets to government services -- according to Wiz Research, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws. Created in the early 1990s, PHP originally stood for "personal home page" but now means "hypertext preprocessor" and sits underneath popular web design platforms. "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," a Wiz blog post said. Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in back-end computer code that have gone unnoticed by humans for years. That has heightened cybersecurity fears, with the number of software vulnerabilities discovered worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total. PHP programmers released a fix Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organizations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline -- a call echoed by authorities from Japan to the European Union. A platform affiliated with China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology urged the same, warning of "two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities with severe impact" in PHP. Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online. Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, described the discovery as "quite devastating." It could allow "attackers to get into your servers without any authorisation, without any username or password," she told AFP. "Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want" -- from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content -- she added, urging institutions to "take it seriously." - 'New phase' - Government agency sites in countries from Australia to Finland and the Netherlands were among those that went dark, while services from insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were under emergency maintenance. Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented, while the foundation that runs Wikipedia warned users they could see outages while it addressed the flaws. "If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post. Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch. Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP's code. OpenAI said the discovery "marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact." Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. The flaws had been reported privately to PHP's developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared. - AI fuels urgency - Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix -- prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them. Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, told AFP that the fear of hackers using AI to quickly and easily exploit the PHP vulnerabilities had fuelled urgency to react. So far there has been little evidence of damaging attacks, although data breaches could lead to a wave of so-called "phishing" attacks, where hackers use personal details to steal passwords, down the line. Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to fix their websites relatively fast, Kerrison said -- but others may be left vulnerable. "There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won't for days, weeks and months," Kerrison warned. That may include user-run blogs that could be weaponised to spread computer viruses, spam people or distribute malicious content, he said. arp-kaf/fox This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/websites-dark-worldwide-ai-exposes-171251949.html

item.title: This Nebraska independent could decide which party controls the Senate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The biggest question heading into November's midterms is whether, once all votes have been counted, Democrats or Republicans will win control of Congress. The final answer, though, might ultimately depend on someone who isn't a member of any party. Dan Osborn is an independent candidate running for Senate in Nebraska. He's challenging Republican incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts in a race that appears on track to be the closest contest the deep-red state has seen in decades. Osborn has consistently been critical of both parties and puts major emphasis on the goal of breaking up their control over American politics. That could make him something of a wild card if he's elected to the nation's most important legislative body. Here's what you need to know about who he is, what he stands for and what he needs to do to pull off an upset in the typically deep-red state of Nebraska. Yahoo Who is Dan Osborn? Osborn grew up in Omaha, Neb., as the son of a railroad worker and a seamstress. When he was 16, his parents moved to Washington state after his father suffered a workplace accident that forced him to transition to a desk job — Osborn chose to stay in Nebraska and live on his own. After graduating from high school, he joined the Navy and served for four years as a storekeeper on the aircraft carrier USS Constellation. After leaving the Navy, he did stints in both the Nebraska and Tennessee National Guards. In 2004, he began working as an industrial mechanic at a factory owned by the Kellogg's cereal company and joined his workplace union — a decision that would ultimately put him on the path to politics. He had risen to president of the union by 2021, when he led his coworkers into a contentious negotiation with the company that eventually resulted in a 77-day strike that became a major national story. Dan Osborn speaks to striking Kellogg's factory workers in 2021. Dan Osborn/Facebook Kellogg's fired him two years later after accusing him of watching Netflix while on the job, a charge he believes was a pretense for retaliating against him for his union activities. He happened to lose his job in the lead-up to an election cycle when both of Nebraska's Senate seats would be on the ballot. Osborn opted to run as an independent against incumbent Republican Sen. Deb Fischer, who was not facing a Democratic challenger. "Seeing how we were getting screwed by our bosses kind of lit a fire under me," he told the American Prospect in 2024. Fischer had won her previous bid for reelection by nearly 20 percentage points and looked to be a shoo-in for another term in the overwhelmingly Republican state. But Osborn's unpolished, everyman style and willingness to criticize both major political parties struck a nerve with voters, raising speculation that he just might have a real chance. By Election Day, polls showed him trailing by as little as a single percentage point. Those surveys proved to overstate how close the contest really was. In the end, Fischer won reelection by about 6.5 points . Though the race didn't end up being particularly close, it was far tighter than Nebraska's other Senate contest that same year. In that race, Ricketts defeated his Democratic challenger by more than 25 percentage points. When Osborn declared his interest in running again this year, Democrats once again chose to give him a clear runway to challenge Ricketts. The Democratic primary winner, Cindy Burbank, promptly withdrew from the race after being named her party's nominee. The Nebraska Democratic Party has urged voters to back Osborn as "the best opportunity to defeat Pete Ricketts." What does he stand for? The question of what Osborn stands for may be just as important as the question of who he will stand with if he gets elected to the Senate. There are currently two independents in the chamber, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Sen. Angus King of Maine. Both of them caucus with the Democrats, which means they generally work with Democrats on Senate business. Osborn has said he will handle things differently. "We're not going to caucus with either party. In fact, we'll caucus with everybody, you could say," he said during a press conference on Oct. 12. "Independent means independent." In an evenly divided Senate, Osborn's vote could be the tiebreaker determining whether a Democrat or Republican serves as majority leader, a position that gives whoever holds it the power to influence which legislation comes to the floor, shape committee leadership and set the chamber's legislative agenda. In terms of policy, one of Osborn's top goals is breaking what he's called the "two-party doom loop" in Washington under Democrats and Republicans. He supports proposals to reduce the influence of money in politics, including overturning Citizens United, banning lawmakers from trading stocks and eliminating "dark money" in elections. He has also called for term limits and an age cap for members of Congress. On social issues, Osborn largely believes in promoting individual freedom. Though he's personally opposed to abortion, he supports restoring the protections established by Roe v. Wade . He's a vocal advocate for gun rights, believes medical marijuana should be legal and wants to enact a nationwide "right to repair" policy for privately owned property. Osborn also supports strong, humane immigration enforcement, reining in government spending, middle-class tax cuts, expanding the Affordable Care Act, breaking up corporate monopolies and ending foreign wars. If elected to the Senate, Osborn's independent streak could make him a key swing vote on a number of important issues, giving him substantial influence over which bills become law. That would be a significant contrast to Ricketts, whose vote aligned with Trump's position 100% of the time last year, according to a tally from Roll Call. What are his chances? Osborn faces a steep challenge in his effort to oust Ricketts, even in a potential blue wave year. There are nearly the same number of registered Republicans in the state as there are voters from all other parties and independents combined. Polling in the Nebraska Senate race has been relatively sparse compared with some of the other higher-profile contests across the country. The few polls that have been released mostly suggest that Osborn remains the underdog. Though one poll last month showed him slightly ahead, two other recent polls have had him behind by 3 to 5 percentage points. At the same time, forecasters are still giving Osborn a genuine chance of winning. Last week, the nonpartisan Center for Politics shifted its rating for the race from Likely Republican to Leans Republican, suggesting the contest might have become tighter. The other major forecaster, the Cook Political Report , still classifies the race as a likely Republican victory. item.title: Peter Thiel breaks with Trump over Iran war: 'We should not have done it'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he’s skeptical of the U.S. war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration’s defining foreign policy decisions. Thiel's remarks, delivered on Oct. 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month. “I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made.” Thiel added, “Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.” In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president. Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict. The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall . In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney. "I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” Thiel said. “And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran." Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the Oct. 7 attack, where he said he asked the leader about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, “I can’t just Dresdenize it,” referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people. The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance’s Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was “skeptical” of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war. Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment. Read more from Thiel’s latest lectures in Thursday’s edition of Decoded by POLITICO , including his sentiments toward Israel and predictions for the 2028 election. item.title: Elon Musk compared Tesla's robot to a toddler. Meta had a different AI surprise.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Earnings season is in full swing, and Big Tech calls are about more than the heavy use of "superintelligence," which some read as a bid to please the White House after it reportedly disliked the term "artificial intelligence." Here are three moments from the earnings calls of Tesla ( TSLA ), Meta ( META ), and IBM ( IBM ) on late Wednesday that stuck with us. Tesla Much of the focus today is on Tesla cutting its capital spending plans for this year to $20 billion from the $25 billion it guided to three months ago. A key factor appears to be that its Optimus robots need more training before they're released into the real world. Elon Musk said investors should think of Optimus as a baby: "A big difference with Optimus versus the cars is we don't have this vast fleet of cars from which we can gather training data. With Optimus, we have to bootstrap it by making the robots and having them do self-play, which is really how a human learns to navigate the world. You can see this when you have a toddler, and they grow up, and initially, they're sort of wobbly, and they don't know how to do things. Eventually they learn to wipe their own ass, which is a big milestone. As anyone who's had kids knows. Then they learn to read and do all sorts of things and be able to do these things. They learn this by playing. We actually need Optimus to play at scale in order to have it be really good at tasks in the real world." Meta Are early users of Meta's ( META ) Muse AI agent overspending? Mark Zuckerberg's comments on credit limits during the earnings call suggest they might be. That raises a bigger question: Could AI agent shopping end badly for retailers and banks, in the form of unpaid debts and write-offs? "The most common use case for Muse is shopping, with more than a quarter of people who are using Muse engaging in this with an average purchase size of over $200," Zuckerberg said on the call. "Plaid told us that they hadn't seen activity like they're seeing with their connector on any other service before. In the first week, we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected." IBM IBM ( IBM ) CEO Arvind Krishna seemed to be in a better place this earnings call compared to three months ago , which came on the heels of a shock earnings warning that sent the stock reeling. It was interesting to hear Krishna call out some C-suite concerns about the current spending on AI tools: "I think what we are seeing is that at least larger enterprises are becoming a lot more cognizant and a lot more aware of what is the true ROI of all of their AI spend. They are also getting worried if some of the AI spending completely out of control with no real return. But the way I have always characterized it is, there is no question to us, and this is the advice I give every C-suite member that I meet, that what we are trying to give people on AI, the productivity, the advantages of AI, the way it is going to change work, is very real. Let me not make any confusion around that." item.title: Russia pounds Kyiv with missiles and drones, hours after agreeing to peace talks
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russia bombarded Kyiv with ballistic missiles in an hourslong nighttime barrage, while the Russian military said Thursday that its air defenses intercepted over 800 drones fired by Ukraine at Moscow and other cities. At least four people were killed in Ukraine and dozens of others were wounded, officials said, in the large-scale attacks that began only hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” on Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations between Russia, Ukraine and the United States . Putin's consent came in talks in St. Petersburg with U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy, Steve Witkoff, who had spoken of a “new momentum” toward peace after meeting Tuesday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway. No date was set for the tripartite talks. Representatives of the three countries held rounds of “technical” talks in the United Arab Emirates and Switzerland in January and February, seeking to lay the groundwork for detailed negotiations. But they reported little progress beyond exchanges of prisoners of war. Russia and Ukraine remain far apart in their terms for stopping the fighting despite U.S. efforts . Zelenskyy says only a meeting of leaders can end the deadlock. As for the prospect of more “technical talks” between delegations: “We’ll see what happens this time.” Zelenskyy sees ‘no change’ in Moscow's attitude Russia’s aerial attacks hit 12 regions of Ukraine overnight, killing at least four people and wounding scores of others, including five children, Zelenskyy said on social media Thursday. Two women aged 50 and 60 were killed and dozens of others wounded in a Russian strike on a market in Lozova, in Ukraine’s northeastern Kharkiv region, said Oleh Syniehubov, head of the regional military administration. Another person was killed in other strikes on Kharkiv, the State Emergency Service said. The Ukrainian capital endured a noisy night as 21 ballistic missiles came in three waves, Zelenskyy said, smashing apartment buildings, energy facilities, a railway station and the Kyiv subway system, shopping malls and businesses. One person was killed in Kyiv. A Russian ballistic missile carrying cluster munitions — bombs that open in the air and release scores of smaller bomblets — targeted downtown Kyiv, said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy. Ukrainians are bracing for the bitterly cold months ahead as the recent escalation in Russian attacks targets the power grid to deny civilians heat, light and running water. Ukraine says Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for an annual campaign Ukrainians describe as “ weaponizing winter. ” The Russian bombardment showed “there has been no real change in (Moscow’s) attitude toward everything that is happening,” Zelenskyy said. Putin mulls attending G20 in Miami, Kremlin says The Ukrainian leader has pleaded with Washington to supply more Patriot air defense ammunition to stop the ballistic missiles, and to heap more sanctions on Russia to pressure Moscow to pursue peace. Instead, Trump has agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia and waived heavy sanctions on Moscow, while U.S. officials say Patriot ammunition is in short supply. Western analysts say Putin wants to cut out Europe and Kyiv and negotiate Ukraine’s future directly with Washington. The Trump administration has also disparaged Europe. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that Putin had received an invitation to attend the G20 summit in Miami in December but hasn’t yet decided whether to go. “The American administration is doing a lot to help a peaceful settlement,” Peskov told reporters. “European capitals are doing nothing to promote a peaceful resolution, and they are doing a great deal to provoke the further escalation of fighting." Ukrainians chide Trump envoy for flattering Putin Witkoff, the Trump envoy who met with Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, was harshly criticized in Ukraine and in the U.S. for praising the Russian leader as a “humanitarian” for ordering the release of a retired American teacher who was imprisoned on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. Assassination attempts against Putin's foes — routinely denied by the Kremlin — have been common during his decades in power. And as the five-year anniversary of Russia’s all-out invasion of its neighbor approaches, aerial strikes have killed thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of soldiers. The latest “brutal” Russian attacks demonstrate “what Russian ‘humanism’ truly sounds like,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “Appeasement, servility, and flattery will not stop this war. Only strength will.” Russia says it intercepted more than 800 Ukrainian drones Russia’s Defense Ministry said that air defenses overnight downed 808 Ukrainian drones, with two people reported wounded. Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 of the drones were fired toward the Russian capital between late Wednesday and early Thursday. Moscow airports temporarily restricted air traffic overnight. The Russian military hit the facilities involved in making and storing drones and cruise missiles and transport infrastructure in Kyiv in overnight strikes, the Defense Ministry said. Infrastructure in the southern port of Odesa and vessels used for the Ukrainian armed forces were also hit, it said. In other developments, the bodies of 252 people, said by Russia to be Ukrainian soldiers, were returned to Ukraine in an exchange, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said Thursday. Russia received 25 bodies of Russian soldiers, Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliyev, a member of a parliamentary coordination group overseeing the exchanges, told RBC news outlet. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/russia-pounds-ukraines-capital-kyiv-071241165.html

item.title: JD Vance told Republicans to stop criticizing Ramaswamy's ad. Some aren't listening.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Vice President Vance defended GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy amid bipartisan criticism of an ad that features the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent. - Clipped From Video Some leading Ohio Republicans began distancing themselves from a controversial new ad from their gubernatorial nominee, Vivek Ramaswamy, even as the president and vice president defended it. Vice President JD Vance warned Republicans on Wednesday not to break ranks over the commercial, telling them to “stop whining” about it. And President Donald Trump, who endorsed Ramaswamy early in the Ohio primary, told reporters at the White House he “didn’t know anything about it” but heard “the mother went very rogue on the daughter.” “It’s a very unusual situation,” Trump said. The viral ad has drawn bipartisan criticism for featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton. In it, Acton’s mother called her daughter a liar and urged voters not to support her. Acton has said she has not seen her mother since she was about 12 years old, when she says the man her mother married sexually abused her. He faced criminal charges and was “declared a fugitive,” Acton said. “I would not have run that ad,” Sen. Jon Husted, a key Ohio Republican who is in one of the country’s most competitive Senate races, said in a statement to the Associated Press published shortly after appearing at a Cincinnati rally with Vance and Ramaswamy. Another top Ohio Republican, Secretary of State Frank LaRose, told the ABC affiliate in Columbus that he “probably wouldn’t run an ad like that.” LaRose is running for state auditor. At least one other GOP candidate in Ohio personally asked Ramaswamy not to air the controversial ad, a GOP operative told CNN. For months, Ramaswamy has largely run behind other candidates in the state in polling, and now there is a sense he could further jeopardize the GOP’s brand with a last-minute stunt to drum up base support, the source said. “Republicans in the state probably couldn’t be more pissed at him,” the operative told CNN. But another GOP operative downplayed the impact Ramaswamy could have, arguing that because he was running behind other candidates already, some of the concerns about him may already be baked in among GOP voters. What Vance said On Wednesday morning, Vance, a former Ohio senator, instructed his fellow Republicans to set aside any reservations about the ad. “Politics is a tough business, and my message to my fellow elected Republicans is if you actually believe in the things you say you believe in, stop whining about an advertisement and go win the race in 13 days,” Vance said at a news conference in Cincinnati. unknown content item - The initial video – which was shared widely on social media, including by the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. – has been roiling the gubernatorial race since it first showed up on social media, bringing the abuse Acton said she suffered at the hands of her stepfather to the forefront. Until Wednesday afternoon, the GOP criticism of the ad was mainly coming from national figures like Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for president in 2024. But the comments by Husted and LaRose began to show cracks in the relative quiet among Ohio Republicans. Asked about the ad at the news conference, Vance declined to weigh in on its appropriateness but said he was “a little bit disgusted” that some Republicans appeared more outraged about it than they are about Democrats and their policies. Speaking later at a rally in Cincinnati that Ramaswamy attended, Vance brought up the ad on his own. He argued it was a justified response because Democrats have used “every dirty trick in the political book” against Ramaswamy. “Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar,” Vance said. Ryan Smith, the former GOP speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, pushed back against Vance’s criticism of fellow Republicans responding to the ad. “Stop normalizing bad behavior and embarrassing the party,” Smith wrote on X . “Ohio deserves better than this!” Ramaswamy’s campaign leaned into the controversy over the ad Tuesday night, announcing it would spend $4 million to run the spot. “She’s lied her entire life,” Donna Arthur says in the minute-long spot. “My daughter needs help, and she can’t help you if she needs help herself. People can change, but first they have to tell the truth, and my daughter still isn’t doing that.” The video was first published widely on Monday night by an Ohio political blogger, D.J. Byrnes, who is known as “The Rooster.” Byrnes told CNN he obtained the video from a voter who saw it as part of a poll and recorded it. On Tuesday morning, Acton’s campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, denouncing the video and linking it to Ramaswamy. “It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said. “After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.” Later Tuesday, Acton’s campaign released a new ad featuring Stearns making similar points. “Shame on Vivek,” he says in the spot. unknown content item - Ad did not initially have political disclaimer Ramaswamy’s campaign initially did not confirm their involvement in the ad Tuesday, saying only that Ohioans “deserve to know” what Acton’s mother says about her daughter. But later in the day, Ramaswamy confirmed, “It is an ad from our campaign.” The incendiary spot will run on TV and streaming platforms, according to a spokesperson for the Ramaswamy campaign, Connie Luck. Axios first reported that news. from social media When it first circulated, the video did not have the standard disclaimer that political ads carry saying who paid for or authorized them, nor did it show up Tuesday morning as a paid ad in the race on AdImpact, the political ad-tracking service. And the first Ramaswamy campaign statement from Luck did not address whether it was responsible for the video. It suggested voters should consider the message from Acton’s mother and repeated her attack, asserting that “we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor.” The statement went on to argue that people who know Acton well — including “her own mother” — “are clearly warning Ohioans not to vote for her.” “Ohioans deserve to know that,” Luck said. An official with V-PAC, the main super PAC backing Ramaswamy, said it did not make the video. CNN has attempted to contact Arthur for more information about how the video came together. Ramaswamy was heckled at a campaign event Tuesday evening by a person appearing to cite the viral video. Within seconds of Ramaswamy taking the stage at a Columbus-area town hall, an audience member rose up and began yelling at him, making a reference to “Amy Acton’s mother” and the abuse that the candidate says she suffered from her mother’s husband at a young age. “Sir, if you want to be patient and you want to ask a question at the end, you’re free to do that,” Ramaswamy said as the man was escorted out. “Thank you for your contribution today.” Speaking with reporters after the event, Ramaswamy took responsibility for the ad and reiterated that voters should take into account what people who know Acton “well” are saying about her. He said he has never met the mother and that she was “not compensated” for the ad. unknown content item - Acton herself weighed in during an interview with WOSU Public Media . “It’s awful to see her this way, and it’s even more incredible to see that my opponent (Ramaswamy) has taken advantage of someone who’s clearly not well, who is older, and this is totally in line with who he is,” Acton said. Her criticism joined the growing chorus. Haley, Ramaswamy’s 2024 primary rival, said the ad was the latest evidence that Ramaswamy is “a bad guy.” “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it,” she wrote on X . Meghan McCain, the daughter of the late Arizona GOP Sen. John McCain, said on X that the ad was “dastardly” and “never should have been created.” Sherrod Brown, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Ohio, said on X that the video was “disgusting” and that Husted should condemn it. The Democratic Governors Association said in a statement that the video was part of a “relentless smear campaign” that Ramaswamy has waged against Acton. Acton and Ramaswamy are locked in one of the most competitive governor’s races in the country, vying to replace term-limited Republican Mike DeWine. The ads in the race have been especially nasty, fueling a controversial decision by Acton to decline to debate Ramaswamy. Republican candidates in the state are preparing for a statewide bus tour starting Friday. DeWine’s office also has not commented on the ad. He defended Acton earlier in the campaign against criticism about Acton’s work as state public health director during the Covid-19 pandemic. A member of DeWine’s Cabinet, Lydia Mihalik, said Tuesday on X that the ad crossed a line. “We can disagree on plenty of things without losing our sense of decency,” said Mihalik, director of the state’s Department of Development. “I don’t have to agree with Amy Acton’s politics to believe that exploiting someone’s childhood trauma is wrong.” Nick Owens, a Republican activist in Ohio, told CNN the ad is “frankly despicable” and would help Acton raise “a lot of money.” Owens, who calls himself a lifelong Republican, is a former county GOP chair in the state who’s been organizing opposition to data centers. Acton, the former Ohio public health director, has spoken before about her estrangement from her mother and hardscrabble childhood. In a 2019 interview with the Youngstown Vindicator , she said her mother married a man when she was between ages 9 and 12 who abused her and who faced criminal charges. The family was living in a tent at a campground outside Youngstown at the time. According to legal documents provided by the Acton campaign, Acton’s allegations against her stepfather emerged in July of 1978 when her father testified to police his daughter was sexually abused by her stepfather. A day later, her stepfather was arrested for rape. He pleaded not guilty but was indicted by a grand jury in September of that year. By October, prosecutors asked for a warrant for his arrest. In the early 1980s, one record shows authorities were still looking for him, but there is no record of any further action in the case. “I was lucky that it got bad enough, because it got me out of there,” Acton told the Vindicator. She said the last time she saw her mother was at the courthouse when she tried to give her a kiss and Acton rejected her. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Lauren Fox and Kit Maher contributed to this report. item.title: Meta strikes deal to keep Zuckerberg in California after wealth tax concerns
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Carlos Méndez Oct 21 (Reuters) - Meta Platforms has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to keep him living in California after the CEO warned he was ‌considering leaving the state that houses the company's headquarters if voters pass a ‌wealth tax proposal next month. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will get non-voting shares he can sell to potentially foot ​a multi-billion-dollar tax bill in the event the proposal is approved, in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California, or wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, Meta said on Wednesday. Zuckerberg, the world's sixth richest person according to Forbes, told Meta he was ‌considering moving his primary residence ⁠outside California because Proposition 40, a ballot measure dubbed the "California wealth tax", could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to ⁠sell voting shares to pay it. Proposition 40, which asks Californians whether to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state's billionaires, is far from certain to pass, political analysts say. The state ​is ​home to as many as 250 billionaires collectively ​worth upwards of $2 trillion. Zuckerberg, who has ‌a net worth of about $240 billion, can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, allowing him to pay a potential tax bill without losing voting control. The company said on Wednesday it will issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively resulting ‌in a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and ​retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control. Meta's long-term forecasts, ​as described in the filing, showed ​it would need to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars" over several ‌years, beginning as early as fall 2026, ​as it expects to ​need capital to finance its AI-related growth plan. The parent of Facebook and Instagram said a special committee of its board concluded it was "critically important" that Zuckerberg remain in ​a leadership role and continue ‌to manage the company from its California headquarters, particularly during what it described ​as "unprecedented challenge and competition in our industry" driven by AI. By Andrew Chung Oct 21 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump's administration asked the US Supreme Court on Wednesday to let it proceed with a plan to build a US-Mexico border ‌barrier in a remote region in West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park. The ‌Justice Department filed an emergency request for the court to lift a federal judge's order halting wall construction in the region ​while a lawsuit against the project brought by an environmental group and other challengers plays out. The Republican president has long touted building or reinforcing barriers along the US-Mexico border as a signature part of his anti-immigration policies. But his administration's push to extend border infrastructure into the national park, around 250 miles (400 ‌km) southeast of El Paso, has ⁠faced opposition from local officials, conservationists and some Texas Republicans. The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a ⁠group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, that says its fragile adobe structure is threatened by the border construction. The plaintiffs challenged a series of waivers issued by the US Department of Homeland ​Security to ​expedite construction of roads and barriers in the Big ​Bend region, avoiding the application of ‌a variety of environmental and conservation laws. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and the current Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who issued the waivers between February and July, found the region to be an "area of high illegal entry," requiring additional barriers to control the border. US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso issued an injunction on October 2 halting the construction. In an opinion issued later, the judge found ‌that the waivers exceeded the authority of Noem and ​Mullin. The Justice Department in its request urged the Supreme Court ​to pause or overturn Cardone's injunction. "Even assuming ​that the secretary's waiver authority implicates a question of 'vast economic and political significance,' ‌Congress did clearly authorize the secretary both ​to build border barriers and ​to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction," the Justice Department wrote. In August, the administration paused construction in Big Bend after the project drew bipartisan criticism over ​its potential impact on the ‌park's landscape and wildlife. Crews had begun clearing land in the park for roads and ​border security infrastructure, prompting protests and lawsuits seeking to halt the work.
